title: Characterizing possible failure modes in physics-informed neural networks
authors_full: Aditi S. Krishnapriyan, Amir Gholami, Shandian Zhe, Robert M. Kirby, Michael W. Mahoney (Krishnapriyan and Gholami equal contribution)
affiliations: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, USA (Krishnapriyan, Gholami); University of California, Berkeley, USA (Krishnapriyan, Gholami, Mahoney); University of Utah, USA (Zhe); International Computer Science Institute, USA (Kirby, Mahoney)
venue: 35th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2021), Sydney, Australia
subdomain: PINN training reliability: failure-mode diagnosis (loss landscape, ill-conditioning of soft PDE constraints) on 1D convection/reaction/reaction-diffusion; remedies are curriculum regularization and sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) time-marching
industry_context: No industry or company named; academic collaboration (LBNL, UC Berkeley, Univ. of Utah, ICSI). Funding: LBNL LDRD DE-AC02-05CH11231, Alvarez Fellowship; AG supported by Samsung SAIT; UCB team by CLTC, AR0, NSF, ONR. Compute acknowledged from Google TPU Research Cloud, Google Cloud, Google Brain, Intel VLAB, Amazon AWS, Intel.
physics_enforced_exact: Framing problem (Eq 1): F(u(x,t)) = 0, x in Omega subset R^d, t in [0,T], with F taxonomized as parabolic/hyperbolic/elliptic. Three enforced cases, all 1D with periodic BCs on x in [0, 2*pi], T = [0,1]: (1) Convection (Eq 5): du/dt + beta*du/dx = 0, u(x,0) = h(x) = sin(x), u(0,t) = u(2*pi,t); analytical solution u = F^{-1}(F(h(x)) e^{-i*beta*k*t}) in the Fourier domain. (2) Reaction (Eq 14, Appendix A): du/dt - rho*u*(1-u) = 0 (the reaction term of Fisher's equation, a semi-linear ODE), Gaussian IC u(x,0) = exp(-(x-pi)^2 / (2*sigma*(pi/5)^2)) (Eq 17, as printed), u(0,t) = u(2*pi,t); analytical solution u = h(x)e^{rho*t} / (h(x)e^{rho*t} + 1 - h(x)). (3) Reaction-diffusion (Eq 10): du/dt - nu*d2u/dx2 - rho*u*(1-u) = 0, u(x,0) = h(x), periodic BCs; reference solution built by Strang splitting into reaction ODE and diffusion step (diffusion has Fourier-domain analytical solution u = F^{-1}(F(u(x,t=t^n)) e^{-nu*k^2*t}), Eq 12).
pde_type: multiple (hyperbolic convection; parabolic reaction-diffusion; semi-linear ODE reaction)
dimensionality: 1D+time (one spatial dimension x in [0, 2*pi], t in [0,1] for all cases)
nonlinearity: mildly nonlinear — convection has a linear PDE constraint (the paper notes this explicitly); reaction and reaction-diffusion add a semi-linear logistic term rho*u*(1-u); no strong nonlinearities, yet PINNs still fail, which is the paper's point
bcs_ic_handled: Periodic boundary conditions for all systems, enforced through an extra term L_B in the loss taking the difference between predicted NN solution at the two domain ends (Eq 8): L_B = (1/N_b) sum_i (u_hat(0, t_i) - u_hat(2*pi, t_i))^2. Initial condition u(x,0) = h(x) enters through the data-fit term (1/N_u) sum (u_hat - u_i^0)^2 evaluated at N_u initial points. No Dirichlet/Neumann spatial BCs.
enforcement_mechanism: soft-penalty — the PDE constraint is imposed as a weighted residual penalty lambda_x*F(u) added to the empirical loss (Eq 3), contrasted in the paper with the hard-constraint formulation min L(u) s.t. F(u)=0 (Eq 2); the paper's central claim is that exactly this soft differential-operator regularization causes the failures
enforcement_details: u_hat = NN(theta, x, t); PDE-operator derivatives (du_hat/dt, du_hat/dx, d2u_hat/dx2) computed by automatic differentiation (PyTorch) and the residual is squared and summed over N_f randomly sampled collocation points with weight lambda_x. Residuals: convection du_hat/dt + beta*du_hat/dx (Eq 7); reaction-diffusion du_hat/dt - nu*d2u_hat/dx2 - rho*u_hat*(1-u_hat) (Eq 13); reaction du_hat/dt - rho*u_hat*(1-u_hat) (Eq 16). No output transforms, projections, or hard constraints. Appendix B analyzes why this regularization is harmful: unlike norm-based regularizers, it involves a differential operator that makes the problem ill-conditioned — approximate condition number O(nu*N^2) for diffusion and O(beta*N) for convection (N = grid size; B.1 derivation; main text p.15 quotes convection as O(beta*N^2)), quadratically scaled because the PINN uses an L2 loss.
network_architecture: 4-layer fully-connected MLP with 50 neurons per layer, used for ALL experiments (Sec. 3 Experiment setup, p.4); seq2seq experiments use 'the exact same NN architecture' as the full space-time PINN. Capacity of this same architecture is shown sufficient to reach the good solution when training is restructured (Sec. 5).
input_representation: (x, t) spatial coordinate and time (general formulation 'takes (x,t), and possibly other quantities, as inputs'; experiments use (x,t) only)
output_representation: solution field u_hat = NN(theta, x, t); no transforms on outputs
loss_terms: General soft-constrained form (Eqs 3-4): min L(u) + lambda_x*F(u), with L(u) = L_avo + L_aus (as printed) measuring the misfit of the NN prediction and the initial/boundary conditions. Convection (Eq 7): L(theta) = (1/N_u) sum_{i=1}^{N_u} (u_hat - u_i^0)^2 + (1/N_f) sum_{j=1}^{N_f} lambda_x*(du_hat/dt + beta*du_hat/dx)^2 + L_B. Reaction-diffusion (Eq 13): L(theta) = (1/N_u) sum (u_hat - u_i^0)^2 + (1/N_f) sum lambda_x*(du_hat/dt - nu*d2u_hat/dx2 - rho*u_hat*(1-u_hat))^2 + L_B. Reaction (Eq 16): same structure with residual du_hat/dt - rho*u_hat*(1-u_hat). Boundary term L_B = (1/N_b) sum (u_hat(0,t_i) - u_hat(2*pi,t_i))^2 (Eq 8).
loss_weighting: fixed scalar lambda_x multiplying the residual sum (inside the collocation sum); no adaptive/NTK/self-adaptive weighting. The paper sweeps lambda_x in {1e-6, 1e-5, 1e-3, 1e-1, 1e1} (Fig E.1) and finds increasing lambda_x makes the loss landscape more complex while error 'stays consistently high' (rel. err 0.60-1.69) — tuning the weight cannot resolve the failure. Difficulty is instead annealed by curriculum over the PDE coefficients (beta, rho).
sampling_strategy: collocation points (x,t) randomly sampled on the domain each training round; counts: 1000 collocation points to predict the entire space-time state space for T=[0,1] (footnote 4), split per time segment for seq2seq with the total budget kept identical (e.g. 100 points per section for dt=0.1); 10,000 collocation points in the Appendix E.3 convection seq2seq comparison for both methods. No adaptive refinement (RAD/RAR).
optimizer_schedule: L-BFGS with learning-rate sweep from 1e-4 to 2.0 (footnote 2); authors note SGD variants 'underperform in comparison to L-BFGS' for PINNs. Every model trained at least 10 times with different preset random seeds; relative and absolute errors averaged. Curriculum: train at low beta (or rho), then use the trained weights to re-initialize the NN and train at progressively higher beta/rho. seq2seq: march in time with dt = 0.05 or 0.1.
training_compute: Not stated per experiment; no training times given. Acknowledgements list computational resources from Google TPU Research Cloud, Google Cloud, Google Brain, Intel VLAB, Amazon AWS, and Intel.
domain_decomposition: None (no cPINN/XPINN-style spatial subdomains or interface conditions). Closest analogue is seq2seq time discretization: the solution is predicted one dt segment at a time (dt = 0.05 or 0.1) and the prediction at t+dt is used as the initial condition for the next segment, with collocation budget held fixed vs the full space-time baseline.
transfer_or_pretraining: Curriculum regularization is a warm-start scheme across problem difficulties: weights trained at lower beta (easier problem) re-initialize the network for training at the next higher beta; likewise over rho for the reaction case (Fig 4a, Sec. 5.1, Fig E.4). Not transfer learning from external data.
uq_method: None. Reliability is instead assessed empirically: at least 10 runs with different preset random seeds per case, with error spread shown (Fig E.2 box plots show curriculum training also decreases the variance of the error, not just the mean).
data_regime: physics-only — no interior observation data; supervision consists of the initial-condition points (data term) plus the periodic-boundary penalty, with collocation points carrying the physics: 'the only data available here is from the PDE itself, i.e., just the initial condition' (Sec. 5.2). Analytical ground-truth solutions used only for evaluation.
datasets_used: Three synthetic 1D benchmarks with closed-form solutions: (1) 1D convection, u(x,0)=sin(x), periodic on x in [0,2*pi], T=[0,1], beta in {1,...,40} (heatmaps up to beta=70); (2) 1D reaction (Fisher reaction term), Gaussian IC, rho swept (tables to rho=10); (3) 1D reaction-diffusion with Strang-splitting reference, rho=5 with nu in {2,...,6} (highlighted failure case rho=5, nu=5).
baselines_compared: Regular/vanilla PINN training on the entire space-time domain at once is the baseline against both remedies (curriculum regularization, seq2seq); self-comparison across lambda_x values; no classical numerical solver (FEM/FVM/spectral) or alternative network architecture is benchmarked.
evaluation_metrics: Relative L2 error L2_rel = (1/N sum_{i=0}^{N} ||u_hat - u||_2) / (1/N sum ||u||_2) and absolute error (1/N) sum ||u_hat - u||_2 (p.4), averaged over >= 10 preset random seeds; loss-landscape visualizations by perturbing the trained model along the first two dominant Hessian eigenvectors (more informative than random directions, citing [41,42]); qualitative exact-vs-predicted heatmaps.
key_quantitative_results:
- Vanilla PINN failure scaling: convection relative error 7.84e-3 (beta=1), 1.08e-2 (beta=10), 7.50e-1 (beta=20), 8.97e-1 (beta=30), 9.61e-1 (beta=40) — 'almost 100% error for beta > 10'; reaction error 'quickly gets to 100%' as rho increases (predicts near-zero homogeneous solution); reaction-diffusion relative error 93% (rho=5, nu=5) and 50% (nu=2).
- Curriculum regularization (Table 1, convection): beta=20 rel err 7.50e-1 -> 9.84e-5; beta=30 8.97e-1 -> 2.02e-2; beta=40 9.61e-1 -> 5.33e-1 — 'by almost two orders of magnitude' (Fig 4), plus reduced error variance (Fig E.2); reaction: 0.1-0.6 orders lower for rho=2-4 and 1-2 orders lower for rho=5-10, capturing sharp features even at rho=10.
- seq2seq time-marching (Table 2, reaction-diffusion rho=5): nu=2: 5.07e-1 -> 1.18e-2 (dt=0.1); nu=5: 9.35e-1 -> 2.36e-2 (dt=0.05); 'almost two orders of magnitude' lower (Fig 6); reaction (Table E.2): rho=10: 9.96e-1 -> 6.88e-2 (dt=0.05); convection (Table E.1, 10,000 collocation pts): beta=30: 7.38e-1 -> 1.05e-1 (dt=0.1).
- Loss landscape (Fig 3): smooth at beta=1, increasingly complex/non-symmetric with larger beta; optimizer stuck in a local minimum with very high loss for large beta; lambda sweep (Fig E.1) shows error stays high (0.60-1.69) for lambda_x from 1e-6 to 1e1.
- Condition-number analysis (App B): soft differential regularization is ill-conditioned — O(nu*N^2) diffusion, O(beta*N) convection — explaining unstable gradients and poor convergence.
speedup_claims: No runtime/efficiency speedup claims; the claim is in accuracy: 'we can achieve up to 1-2 orders of magnitude lower error with these methods as compared to regular PINN training' (abstract); curriculum for the beta=30 convection case improves 'by almost two orders of magnitude' (Fig 4); seq2seq for reaction/reaction-diffusion 'almost two orders of magnitude' (Fig 6, p.10).
ablations: (1) Loss-landscape study vs beta (Fig 3): perturbation along top-2 Hessian eigenvectors shows smooth landscape at beta=1 becoming complex/non-symmetric at beta=20-40, with the optimizer stuck in a high-loss local minimum — soft PDE regularization is the cause. (2) lambda_x sweep (Fig E.1): increasing lambda_x makes the landscape more complex and error stays high; reducing lambda_x also fails (poor solutions violating the PDE). (3) Expressivity check (Sec. 5): the SAME 4x50 tanh MLP finds the good solution under curriculum training, proving failure is optimization difficulty, not network capacity. (4) Curriculum across regimes (Table 1, Fig E.2, Fig E.4): 1-2 orders error reduction and lower variance vs vanilla. (5) seq2seq vs full space-time with identical architecture and identical total collocation budget (footnote 4): lower error in every tested beta/rho/nu regime (Tables 2, E.1, E.2). (6) Condition-number derivations (App B.1) for convection and diffusion residual operators.
stated_limitations: (1) Toy scope: conclusions drawn from two fundamental 1D PDE problems (convection, diffusion/reaction) with analytical solutions; 'we picked two fundamental PDE problems of diffusion and convection and showed that the PINN only works for very simple cases' (Conclusions, p.10). (2) 'it may require extensive hyperparameter tuning which is often not feasible in practice' for vanilla PINNs, and curriculum requires per-regime scheduling of beta/rho (Sec. 3.1, p.5). (3) seq2seq results are 'initial results ... promising'; 'further developments may lead to still better ways of using PINNs and learning PDEs', including more sophisticated timestep prediction and seq2seq approaches (p.10). (4) 'the condition number is only one of the many factors involved in this problem' — function complexity, non-convex landscape, and optimizer limitations must also be considered (App B, p.15). (5) Condition-number bounds are approximate because nonlinearity makes behavior state-dependent (App B.1, p.15). (6) Instability expected to worsen 'in the presence of noise, or cases with non-trivial physics' (App B, p.15).
failure_modes: THE central topic of the paper. (1) Vanilla PINNs achieve near-100% relative error on 1D convection for beta >= 10 (learn the BCs but fail past a certain timestep, predicting a flat/homogeneous field); (2) reaction: error jumps to 100% as rho grows, network predicts a mostly homogeneous near-zero solution; (3) reaction-diffusion: 50-93% relative error, unable to capture 'sharp' and/or diffusive features; (4) root cause A: the PDE-based soft constraint makes the loss landscape non-smooth and complex (worse for larger coefficients and larger lambda_x), trapping L-BFGS in poor local minima; (5) root cause B: ill-conditioning of the differential regularization operator (diffusion O(nu*N^2), convection O(beta*N)) leading to large gradients and unstable behavior — explicitly connected to the gradient-pathology literature [35]; (6) explicitly NOT a capacity problem: the same architecture succeeds under curriculum; (7) learning the entire space-time at once is harder than time-marching (ill-conditioned mapping over the full horizon); (8) related-work failures cited: stiff ODEs in chemical kinetics [15], heterogeneous media [7], certain fluid flows [10], high-frequency targets via NTK analysis [36,37], imbalanced back-propagated gradients [35].
reproducibility: Open-source framework built on top of PyTorch, released 'to help with reproducibility and also to enable other researchers to extend the results': https://github.com/a1k12/characterizing-pinns-failure-modes (ref [26]; printed as a mangled citation '[26] C. possible failure modes...'). Protocols stated: >= 10 preset random seeds per config, averaged; L-BFGS learning-rate sweep 1e-4 to 2.0; collocation counts partially given (1000 main text footnote; 10,000 App E.3). No per-run hardware, timings, or full hyperparameter tables.
quotable_finding: We provide evidence that the soft regularization in PINNs, which involves PDE-based differential operators, can introduce a number of subtle problems, including making the problem more ill-conditioned. (p. 1)
relevance_rqs: RQ2: training-strategy components — optimizer choice (L-BFGS vs SGD), loss weighting (lambda sweep), curriculum scheduling, seq2seq time-marching, seed-variance reporting; RQ3: the soft-penalty autodiff-residual mechanism itself is shown to be the failure source (ill-conditioning, landscape complexity); RQ4: the canonical quantitative evidence for the reliability/failure-modes discussion of PINNs; RQ1: not evidenced (no industry application).
manuscript_section: S4 methods (PINN training failure modes, loss-landscape/conditioning diagnostics, curriculum + seq2seq remedies); RQ4 reliability/limitations discussion; T2-T3 (training-strategy error-comparison numbers); F5/F6-style figures (loss landscapes, exact-vs-predicted failure heatmaps)
cross_paper_links: builds-on: PINN-A01 (Raissi, Perdikaris, Karniadakis 2019 = ref [28]; 'The original PINN approach of [28] trains the NN model to predict the entire space-time at once' — the baseline formulation diagnosed here). compares-to / discusses: NTK failure analyses (ref [37] Wang, Yu & Perdikaris 'When and why PINNs fail to train: a neural tangent kernel perspective' = PINN-A06; ref [36] eigenvector bias of Fourier feature networks); gradient pathologies and learning-rate annealing (ref [35] Wang, Teng & Perdikaris, arXiv:2007.14536 — the weighting line related to PINN-A07's self-adaptive weights); Stiff-PINN for stiff chemical kinetics (ref [15]); Fuks & Tchelepi limitations for nonlinear two-phase transport (ref [10]); curriculum learning (ref [1] Bengio et al. 2009) as the ML concept transplanted to PDE difficulty; predecessor methods Lagaris et al. 1998 (ref [18]) and PDE-Net (ref [19]).
notes_caveats: All benchmarks are 1D+time toy problems with known analytical solutions; the loss-landscape evidence is local (perturbation along the top-2 Hessian eigenvectors of one trained model). Internal inconsistency: main text p.15 states the convection condition number scales as O(beta*N^2), while the Appendix B.1 derivation and p.16 state convection scales as O(beta*N) (diffusion O(nu*N^2)) — cite the appendix version. The remedies are training-procedure-level only: no comparison against classical solvers, Fourier-feature/adaptive architectures, or adaptive sampling. Gains are largest exactly where the baseline collapses; curriculum does NOT fully fix the hardest case (beta=40 rel err still 5.33e-1) and convection seq2seq gains are modest (7.38e-1 -> 1.05e-1) compared with the near-total fixes on reaction-diffusion. lambda sweep shows neither small nor large lambda resolves the failure, reinforcing that weighting alone is insufficient. The ~2114 citations reflect its status as the canonical PINN failure-mode diagnosis paper rather than benchmark breadth.
